decisions.what: Which name does the README give each thing, and where does the reader learn a word of Lane's?
decisions.decided: The UX's names: a rule (a sentence in a step, with a check of it), the check script (the one script lay.py puts into the plugin), the orchestrator (the subagent that starts the others), the flow (the order it starts them in). Each is said in everyday words where the reader first meets it. Lane is written with a capital. lay.py's own output calls a rule a lane and its check a hook; the walkthrough says so once, where the reader first meets that output.

decisions.what: What is Lane, in one sentence?
decisions.decided: Lane is a Claude Code plugin that checks the subagents of your plugin, so that they keep the rules of their steps and start one another in the order that you set.
grounds: The kind the reader places it among is a Claude Code plugin; the two halves are the UX's O1 and O2, dev/lane/ux.md:11 and 28.

decisions.decided: Your subagents keep the rules of their steps on every run, and your orchestrator starts them in your order, which you write as a flow. You write no code for the checks and no script for the order.
grounds: dev/lane/ux.md:11-12: "O1: The developer AI has its subagents keep the rules of their steps on every run, with no check code of its own."
dev/lane/ux.md:28-29: "O2: The developer AI has its orchestrator start the other subagents in the order of its flow on every run, with no script of its own for the order."

decisions.what: What does Lane do that another way of doing the same work does not?
decisions.decided: A rule is a sentence in a step with a check of it. When a subagent breaks the rule, the check stops the call and shows the subagent the same sentence, headed by the plugin's name. A hook that only refuses a call leaves the subagent to look for another way; a subagent that sees the sentence of its own step goes back to the step. The idea has no figure of its own: its two parts, the sentence and the check, are drawn in How it works.
grounds: dev/lane/architecture.md:17-20: "The check script shows a stopped subagent the sentence of the rule, after the plugin's name. A subagent whose call is only refused tries another way; one that sees its own step goes back to it (KR1.3)."

decisions.what: What might the reader expect of Lane that it does not do?
decisions.decided: Six non-goals: it checks only subagents with rules, not the main conversation or a skill, so the orchestrator of a flow must be a subagent; it is no security boundary, so what must never happen is blocked by GitHub's branch protection or Claude Code's permission rules; it sees tool calls and ends of work, not what a subagent thinks; it does not read every form of a shell command, and stops a command that names a file in a way it cannot follow, asking for the plain path; it does not choose the next subagent from a run's results, as a flow is a fixed order that goes back only on an answer you name; it reads your plugin's texts in one format, and another format needs an adapter.

decisions.what: Which promise of the opening does each line of How it works keep, and what changes in the figure?
decisions.decided: The figure keeps its boxes and lines: lay.py writes each rule's sentence into its step and copies the check script into the plugin (no code written); Claude Code sends each tool call and end of work to the check script, which stops a break and shows the sentence again (rules kept, the idea) and tells the orchestrator which subagent to start next (order kept). The reader's box, "you, the developer", becomes "you (an AI)", as the README speaks to an AI and names the subagent's box the same way.
